<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases and executed the Q&A format cleanly, making this genuinely close. But PRO's core structural argument — that natural-monopoly, thin-market goods (rural transit, broadband, hospitals) resist fixing via cash because fixed infrastructure costs don't respond to individual purchasing power — went under-rebutted. CON's answer ("cash fails under the current regime, not guaranteed purchasing power") was asserted rather than defended, and CON's own concession that public systems also abandon rural routes undercut its "demand creates supply" claim without establishing that cash does better. PRO's "rationed by need vs. rationed by price" and "degraded service vs. zero service" framings, deployed cleanly in answer to the pressure questions, gave PRO a sharper, more defensible tiebreaker heading into the close. CON's cleverest move — flipping PRO's own "welfare states layer cash on services" point into a concession of the motion — was a strong rebuttal, but PRO's closing largely ignored it rather than directly answering, which is a real but not fatal gap. On balance PRO's mechanism (natural monopoly / thin-market failure) proved more resilient under cross-examination than CON's mechanism (cash reliably induces supply), giving PRO a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question on rural broadband/hospitals persisting despite "guaranteed demand" (A3.2), and CON's comparatively thin answer blaming "the current regime" (B4.3) while conceding public systems fail rural areas too — this exchange exposed the weakest link in CON's demand-creates-supply mechanism and was never fully repaired.</best_rebuttal>
